opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so for me, MiniChart was really a proof point for something we'd been arguing for a while, which is that a lot of the gains people chase through scale can actually come from being much more thoughtful about the data.

The setup was pretty simple. Chart question-answering is a task where you need the model to actually read a visual: pull values off axes, compare bars, follow trend lines, sometimes do a little arithmetic on top. The default approach is to take a big general-purpose vision-language model and hope it's seen enough charts along the way. What we wanted to show is that you don't need that. If you carefully construct the training data, you can get a much smaller model that's competitive on this task, and sometimes better than models many times its size.

The interesting part was how much the curation mattered. It wasn't just "get more chart data." It was about diversity: different chart types, styles, and question types, from simple lookups to multi-step reasoning. It was about quality: filtering out examples where the question is ambiguous or the answer is wrong, because a few bad examples teach the model bad habits fast. And it was about coverage, deliberately going after the failure modes we saw instead of just sampling whatever was easy to generate. A lot of that was synthetic, generated with larger models and then filtered and verified. So the pipeline became the product, more than any modeling trick.

The broader lesson, and the reason I keep coming back to it, is that data curation is still under-appreciated relative to architecture and scale. Everybody wants to talk about the model, but for specific tasks, a small model trained on really well-curated data can be cheaper, faster, easier to deploy, and just as good. That's a big deal for companies that don't want to call a frontier model for every request.

And honestly, that's a lot of why I've gotten so excited about tooling for this. Curation today is still pretty artisanal. People write one-off scripts and it's hard to reproduce. MiniChart convinced me that if we can make high-quality data curation systematic and repeatable, we unlock a whole class of small, specialized models that punch well above their weight.

r001.rationale: The response says a smaller model can be competitive or sometimes outperform much larger models, but it does not identify a 7B model or say it reached Claude 3.5 and Gemini 1.5 performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so MiniChart is a good example of what we've been trying to show at Bespoke Labs, which is that the data matters a lot more than people tend to give it credit for. The task is chart question answering: you give the model an image of a chart, a bar chart or a line plot or whatever, and you ask it a question about it. And what we found is that you can take a pretty small open model, on the order of three billion parameters, and if you're really careful about the data you train it on, you can get it to match or beat models that are significantly larger, including some of the closed frontier models on this specific task.

And the key word there is careful. It wasn't about scraping a huge pile of chart images off the internet and throwing them at the model. It was about generating synthetic data in a way where we controlled the diversity of chart types, the kinds of questions, the reasoning that's required to answer them, and then filtering aggressively. A lot of the work was actually in throwing data away. If the question was ambiguous, or the answer wasn't actually derivable from the chart, or the reasoning trace had an error in it, that goes. Because a small model will happily learn your mistakes, and it has less capacity to average them out than a large one does.

So I think the demonstration is twofold. One, for a well-scoped task, curation can substitute for scale to a degree that surprises people. You don't need a frontier-sized model to do chart QA really well. And two, data curation is an engineering discipline, not a one-time cleanup step. The pipeline we built for MiniChart, generate, verify, filter, iterate, is the same pattern that we think applies to most domains, and honestly that's a big part of why we open-sourced the tooling around it. The model is almost the byproduct. The reusable thing is the process for making the data good.

r001.rationale: The response says a roughly 3B model can match or beat larger models, including closed frontier models, but it does not identify Claude 3.5 or Gemini 1.5, and it does not say MiniChart used a 7B model.

astra-6.text:
I think MiniChart demonstrates that the quality of the data can matter as much as the size of the model. With chart question answering, you want a model to do more than read a label—you want it to compare values, understand relationships, and reason about what the chart is showing. So the examples you train on need to exercise those abilities.

Data curation is really about making deliberate choices: What do we want the model to learn? Are those cases represented? Are the answers reliable? A smaller model trained on well-chosen data can be surprisingly capable. The takeaway is that improving the data is a powerful way to improve the model, alongside scaling it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think MiniChart demonstrates that the quality of the data can matter more than the size of the model. With chart question answering, you want to be deliberate about the examples you include: the types of charts, the questions you ask, and whether answering those questions actually requires understanding the chart rather than exploiting some shortcut.

If you curate that data well, a smaller model can become surprisingly capable. So the lesson for me is that data curation isn’t just cleaning up a dataset at the end. It’s thinking carefully about what you want the model to learn and building the data around that.
